voice: Say it LOUD. Say it WRONG. But SAY IT.

rooms.title: The Entrance
rooms.label: Warm-Up
rooms.content:
Two periods, one lab 🧪 Today the matter does the work — ice, water and steam are the same substance in three states, and a scientist needs three things to prove it: a fair test, a prediction, and a record.

  • Eight words for the states and the changes between them
  • What melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing actually do to the particles
  • The one rule of a fair test — change one thing
  • A puddle that disappears without ever boiling

rooms.title: The Science Room
rooms.label: Scene
rooms.content:
Minh: Sir, my ice is gone. It was a solid when the bell rang — now it is just water in the cup 🧊
Teacher: Good. So what happened to it? Use the word, not the story.
Minh: It melted. It changed from solid to liquid.
Linh: Mine is still ice. I put mine in the cool bag — so mine stayed a solid.
Teacher: Same substance, two cups, one difference. Linh, what did you change?
Linh: The temperature. Just the temperature. Everything else was the same.
Teacher: Then Linh has run a fair test, and Minh has run a puddle. Write both down.
🤔 Reality check: nothing was added and nothing was lost — the water is still there, in a different state. Melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing are not new substances. They are the same substance with a new state.

rooms.title: The Group Chat
rooms.label: Text Scene
rooms.content:
Linh: ok real question. If ice and steam are both water why do we have four words for it 😤
Nam: bc theyre different STATES. solid liquid gas
Minh: and the words tell you which way it went. melt = solid → liquid. freeze = liquid → solid
Nam: and evaporate = liquid → gas. condense = gas → liquid
Linh: ok that actually makes sense. whats the fair test thing then
Minh: change ONE thing. keep everything else the SAME. then you know what did it
Linh: 🙌 so my cool bag was the one thing
Pro Tip: in an experiment, say the sentence out loud before you start — "I am changing only the _____, and I predict that _____." If you cannot fill both blanks, the test is not fair yet.

rooms.title: The Words
rooms.label: Learn
rooms.content:
1. solid: the state that keeps its own shape — ice, a pencil, a stone. Particles locked tightly in place.
2. liquid: the state that takes the shape of its container — water in a cup, still the same amount.
3. gas: the state that spreads out to fill the whole room — steam, air, the smell of food.
4. melt: solid → liquid, when it is heated. Ice melts on the desk.
5. freeze: liquid → solid, when it is cooled. Water freezes in the freezer.
6. evaporate: liquid → gas, without boiling. The puddle disappears on a warm day.
7. condense: gas → liquid, when it cools. Steam becomes drops on a cold window.
8. fair test: changing only ONE thing and keeping every other thing the same, so the result means something.

rooms.title: A Fair Test
rooms.label: Investigation
rooms.content:
The question: does sugar dissolve faster in hot water than in cold water?

Plan A. Put two spoons of sugar in hot water and stir quickly. Put five spoons of sugar in cold water and do not stir. The hot water wins. Result: useless. You changed the temperature and the amount of sugar and the stirring — you have no idea which one did it.

Plan B. Put two spoons of sugar in 200 ml of hot water. Put two spoons of sugar in 200 ml of cold water. Stir both, the same way, for the same time. Only one thing differs: the temperature. Now the hot water wins and you can say why.
🤔 Reality check: an unfair test does not give a wrong answer — it gives no answer. The only difference between the two plans is the number of things that changed at once.

rooms.title: The Puddle
rooms.label: Reading
rooms.content:
At break time there is a puddle beside the stairs. It is 31 degrees. By 3 o'clock the puddle is gone — but nobody boiled it, and the sun never touched that corner.

What happened: the water evaporated. Fast-moving particles at the surface escaped into the air as a gas. The puddle did not need to boil; it only needed to be warm and open to the air.

Now watch the window of the air-conditioned room. There are drops of water on the inside of the glass, and nobody sprayed anything. The water vapour in the warm air met the cold glass and condensed — gas → liquid, the other direction.
Watch For: evaporate and condense are the quiet pair. No boiling, no freezing, no obvious drama — just a state change you have to notice, not hear.

rooms.title: Game 1 — State Scramble
rooms.label: Game 1
rooms.content: How to win: the letters are shuffled. Click them in the right order to rebuild the word, and read the meaning when it lands. Eight words, no time limit — but the clock in your head is running 😄

rooms.title: Game 2 — State & Change
rooms.label: Game 2
rooms.content: How to win: click the change on the left, then the state it starts from on the right. Wrong pairs shake and let go — guess boldly.

rooms.title: Game 3 — Which Change?
rooms.label: Game 3
rooms.content: One word per bucket: MELTING is solid → liquid · FREEZING is liquid → solid · BOILING is liquid → gas, with bubbles and heat.

rooms.title: The Test
rooms.label: Test
rooms.content:
Scenario: Minh's ice turns to water on the desk before the bell. What is the change called?
Scenario: You want to know whether hot water dissolves sugar faster. Which rule makes it a fair test?
Scenario: A puddle beside the stairs is gone by 3 o'clock, on a warm day, with no heat and no bubbles. What happened to the water?

rooms.title: The Key
rooms.label: Mastery
rooms.content:
🧪 You can now talk like a scientist
  • One substance, three states: ice · water · steam — and the state is decided by heat, not by the substance.
  • Four directions, four words: melt = solid → liquid · freeze = liquid → solid · evaporate = liquid → gas · condense = gas → liquid.
  • Evaporate and condense are the quiet pair: no boiling, no freezing — the change happens at the surface, and you have to notice it.
  • A fair test changes ONE thing: "I am changing only the _____, and I predict that _____." If you cannot say both blanks, the test is not fair.
  • Say the prediction before the result: a scientist who writes the guess down first cannot quietly change it afterwards.
Level Up: tonight, find one change of state in your own house — the freezer, the kettle, a glass of cold water — and say the sentence to somebody: "This is a ____ change: it went from ___ to ___." Two states, one word, out loud. That is the whole lesson, applied.
Write it down: describe your own fair test in two or three sentences. Name the ONE thing you would change, say what you predict, and name one thing you would keep the same.
